doc.title: Expressions and Operators
doc.para: True and False Some operators handle true or false (boolean values). If the result of the operation is 0, it is false; if it is non-zero, it becomes true. When truthiness is evaluated for a string, an empty string is false. Otherwise, an attempt is made to convert it to a number: if successful, the truthiness depends on that numeric value, and if it fails, it becomes false.
Operators Below, operators are explained in order from lowest to highest precedence.

if Operator The if operator if evaluates the expression on the left only if the result of evaluating the expression on the right is true.
a=b if b!=0; // assigns b to a if b is not 0
You cannot obtain the result of the operator.

Sequential Operator The sequential operator , (comma) evaluates the expression on the left, and then evaluates the expression on the right. It does nothing else. The value of the overall operator is the result of evaluating the expression on the right. If multiple commas are written sequentially, they are evaluated in order from left to right.
c = (a=1, b=2); // a=1, b=2 are evaluated, and 2 is assigned to c a=1, b=2, c=3; // evaluated in the order of a=1, b=2, c=3

Assignment Operators The assignment operators are as follows:
= <-> &= |= ^= -= += %= /= \= *= ||= &&= >>= <<= >>>=
Among these, the = operator is a simple assignment operator that assigns the result of evaluating the right side to the left side, and the value of the overall operator is the result of evaluating the right side.
a = 0; // assigns 0 to a a = b = c = 0; // assigns 0 in order of c, b, a
The <-> operator performs a swap. First, it evaluates the left side, then evaluates the right side. After that, it assigns the result of evaluating the right side to the left side, and the result of evaluating the left side to the right side. You cannot obtain the result of the operator. Currently, the left and right expressions are each evaluated twice: once to get the expression's value and once to assign to the expression. Since this specification may change in the future, please do not write code that relies on the number of evaluations.
All other operators take the form operator=, and writing A operator= B means A = A operator B. The value of the overall operator is the result of the operation.

Conditional Operator The conditional operator ? : is a ternary operator. Written in the form A ? B : C, it evaluates A, and if true, evaluates B and ignores C. If false, it evaluates C and ignores B. The value of the overall operator is the value of whichever of B or C was evaluated.
The conditional operator can be used as an lvalue.
a = b==0 ? c : b; // if b is 0, assign c to a; if b is not 0, assign b to a b==0 ? (a=c) : (a=b); // same meaning as above (a ? b : c ) = d; // if a is true, assign d to b; if a is false, assign d to c (example used as an lvalue)

Logical OR Operator The logical OR operator || first evaluates the left side; if true, it ignores the right side, and the overall operator result is true. If the evaluation of the left side is false, it evaluates the right side, and the truth value of that result becomes the overall result of the operator.

Logical AND Operator The logical AND operator && first evaluates the left side; if false, it ignores the right side, and the overall operator result is false. If the evaluation of the left side is true, it evaluates the right side, and that result becomes the overall result of the operator.

Bitwise OR Operator The bitwise OR operator | performs a bitwise logical OR. It evaluates the left side and then the right side, treats the results as integers, and the bitwise OR of them becomes the value of the overall operator.

Bitwise XOR Operator The bitwise XOR operator ^ performs a bitwise logical XOR. It evaluates the left side and then the right side, treats the results as integers, and the bitwise XOR of them becomes the value of the overall operator.

Bitwise AND Operator The bitwise AND operator & performs a bitwise logical AND. It evaluates the left side and then the right side, treats the results as integers, and the bitwise AND of them becomes the value of the overall operator.

Equality and Identity Operators == != === !== are equality/identity operators.
== operator The == operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. If both match, the overall operator is true; if not, it is false. If the types resulting from the evaluations on both sides differ, they are converted appropriately before comparison. For example, -1 == '-1' is true.
!= operator The != operator is the inverted truth value of the == operator.
=== operator The === operator is called the identity comparison operator. It is the same as the == operator, but type conversion is not performed, and it will not evaluate to true unless the types also match.
!== operator The !== operator is the inverted truth value of the === operator.

Comparison Operators < > <= >= are comparison operators.
< operator The < operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. It is true if the result of evaluating the left side is less than the result of evaluating the right side, and false otherwise.
> operator The > operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. It is true if the result of evaluating the right side is less than the result of evaluating the left side, and false otherwise.
<= operator The <= operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. It is true if the result of evaluating the left side is less than or equal to the result of evaluating the right side, and false otherwise.
>= operator The >= operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. It is true if the result of evaluating the right side is less than or equal to the result of evaluating the left side, and false otherwise.
If both items being compared are strings, the comparison is made in wide character code order (usually UNICODE).

Bitwise Shift Operators >> << >>> are bitwise shift operators.
>> operator The >> operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. The result of the overall operator is the left result treated as an integer, signed bit-shifted to the right by the number of times given by the right result.
<< operator The << operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. The result of the overall operator is the left result treated as an integer, bit-shifted to the left by the number of times given by the right result.
>>> operator The >>> operator is the same as the >> operator, but treats the result of evaluating the left side as an unsigned integer.

Addition and Subtraction Operators + - are the addition and subtraction operators, respectively.
+ operator The + operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. If both results are numeric values, numeric addition is performed to produce the overall operator result. If either or both are strings, string addition (concatenation) is performed, resulting in a string where the right result is appended to the left result. Numbers are converted to strings, and object types are converted to strings if possible.
- operator The - operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. Then, the right result is subtracted from the left result as numbers, becoming the value of the overall operator.

Multiplication, Division, and Modulo Operators % / \ * are the modulo, division, integer division, and multiplication operators, respectively.
% operator The % operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. After that, the remainder of dividing the left by the right becomes the value of the overall operator. Both values are treated as integers.
/ operator The / operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. After that, the value of dividing the left by the right becomes the value of the overall operator. Values are treated as real numbers.
\ operator The \ operator performs division like the / operator, but the values are treated as integers.
* operator The * operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. After that, the value of multiplying the left by the right becomes the value of the overall operator. Values are treated as real numbers.

General Unary Operators All of the following are unary operators (with the exception of instanceof).
! operator The prefix ! operator is the logical NOT operator. The value of the overall operator is the inverted truth value of evaluating the expression on the right.
~ operator The ~ operator is the bitwise NOT operator. It evaluates the expression on the right as an integer, performs bitwise negation (1 -> 0, 0 -> 1), and that becomes the value of the overall operator.
-- operator The prefix -- operator is the prefix decrement operator. It subtracts 1 from the item on the right, and the value after subtraction becomes the value of the overall operator.
++ operator The prefix ++ operator is the prefix increment operator. It adds 1 to the item on the right, and the value after addition becomes the value of the overall operator.
new operator The new operator causes the function evaluation expression on the right to create an object instead of performing a function call.
invalidate operator The invalidate operator evaluates the right side and invalidates the resulting object. If the item on the right is void, a string, a number, or an octet sequence, it does nothing. If the object is already invalidated, it also does nothing. If null is specified, an exception is raised.
isvalid operator The isvalid operator evaluates the item on the right or left, returning true if the resulting object is valid, and false if invalid. Placing the operator before or after the evaluation target has the same meaning. If the target is void, a string, a number, or an octet sequence, it always returns true. If null is specified, an exception is raised.
delete operator The delete operator deletes the object member or local variable written on the right side. Returns true if deletion succeeds, false if it fails.
typeof operator The typeof operator evaluates the item on the right and returns the following string depending on its type: void: "void", integer: "Integer", real number: "Real", object: "Object", string: "String", octet sequence: "Octet". However, if an object member is specified and the member does not exist, it becomes "undefined".
# operator The # operator evaluates the item on the right, and the character code of the first character of the string becomes the value of the overall operator.
$ operator The $ operator evaluates the item on the right, treats the result as a character code, and the single character it represents becomes the value of the overall operator.
+ operator The unary + operator evaluates the item on the right. If the item on the right is a real number or an integer, it does nothing. Otherwise, it attempts to convert it to a real number or numeric value, and that result becomes the overall operator result. When attempting to convert a string to a numeric value, if conversion fails, no exception is raised and it becomes 0. If it is a real representation containing a decimal point, it is converted to a real number; otherwise, to an integer. If the string starts with 0x, 0b, or 0, it is interpreted as hexadecimal, binary, or octal, respectively.
- operator The unary - operator evaluates the item on the right, treats the result as a numeric value, and negates its sign to become the overall operator result.
& operator The unary & operator changes access to an object member written on the right side to access the property object itself, without going through property handlers. For example, in propobj = &obj.prop;, the property handler for obj's member property prop is not invoked, and a reference to the member property prop's property object itself is assigned to propobj. Behavior is undefined if the right side is not a property access.
* operator The unary * operator invokes the property handler of the object written on the right side. An expression representing a property object must be written on the right side. For example, *propobj = 1; invokes the setter handler of propobj (which is a property object) and assigns 1.
instanceof operator The instanceof operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. Write something that evaluates to a string representing a class name on the right side; if the left side is an instance of that class, it returns true, otherwise false.

para.ptitle: Function Calls, Parentheses/Brackets, Postfix Increment/Decrement, etc.

dl.dd: The ( ) operator changes operator precedence, or performs a function call.

The [ ] operator is the indirect member selection operator. When written as A [ B ], A is evaluated first, then B is evaluated. Treating B as a string, it searches A for that member name, and the overall operator becomes an access to that member. When used as an lvalue, it also has the effect of creating member B in the object if it does not already exist.

The . operator is the direct member selection operator. When written as A.B, A is evaluated. It searches A for B, and the overall operator becomes an access to that member. When used as an lvalue, it also has the effect of creating member B in the object if it does not already exist.If the left side of the . operator is omitted, it refers to a member in the global object if outside a with statement, or a member of the object specified by that with statement if inside a with statement.
The postfix ++ operator is the postfix increment operator. It adds 1 to the item on the left, and the value of the overall operator becomes the item on the left before addition.
The postfix -- operator is the postfix decrement operator. It subtracts 1 from the item on the left, and the value of the overall operator becomes the item on the left before subtraction.

The postfix ! operator is the expression evaluation operator. It treats the result of evaluating the item on the left as a string and interprets it as an expression string. The result is the value evaluated from interpreting that expression string. The expression operates on the this context (the this at the location where this operator was used).

The incontextof operator evaluates the left side first, then evaluates the right side. Taking the result of evaluating the left side as an object, the overall result of the operation is that object with its context portion replaced by the result of evaluating the right side.
The int operator evaluates the item on the right, and converting it to an integer type becomes the overall result of the operator. It can also be written C-style cast as (int).
The real operator evaluates the item on the right, and converting it to a real number type becomes the overall result of the operator. It can also be written C-style cast as (real).
The string operator evaluates the item on the right, and converting it to a string type becomes the overall result of the operator. It can also be written C-style cast as (string).
